power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Red Tears. Blue Dreams: The Freudian Defense Mechanisms and Object Relations in Jimmy Alcantara's Paired Narratives (Red ang Luha ni Michael and Blue ang Kobre Kama ni Jake)

author.affiliation:
Advance Education Program
								College of Education
								Carlos Hilado Memorial State University
								
									Talisay City Negros Occidental

text.text: This study examines Jimmy Alcantara's Red ang Luha ni Michael and Blue ang Kobrekama ni Jake through a psychoanalytic lens, focusing on the manifestation of denial, displacement, fantasy, and projection in thoughts, emotions, and behaviors of Ricky.

Using a qualitative literary analysis through the literary lens of psychoanalytic approach, the study applies the Hierarchy of Defense Mechanisms and Defense Mechanism Rating Scales Q-Sort (DMRS-Q) framework of Di Giuseppe and Perry (2021) as the basis for identifying and interpreting defensive patterns in the narratives.
Object Relations Theory serves as a complementary perspective in examining Ricky's emotional attachment to Michael and the psychological significance of objects associated with their relationship.

The findings reveal that Ricky employs denial in resisting threatening realities, displacement in redirecting emotional conflict toward objects and his surroundings, fantasy in constructing an idealized family through Jake, and projection in attributing his psychological conflict to Michael.

The analysis further demonstrates that the scarlet paint, transformed apartment, blue bedspread, and Jake transcend their material functions and become symbolic extensions of Ricky's emotional attachment and desire for intimacy, stability, and belonging.

Altogether, the findings suggest that Alcantara portrays psychological conflict through the interaction of defensive processes and symbolic attachment, gradually blurring the boundary between Ricky's internal desires and external reality.

The study contributes to a psychoanalytic reading of contemporary Filipino literature by demonstrating how defense mechanisms and object relations can illuminate the representation of emotional dependency, attachment, and psychological fragmentation in literary narratives.
Literature has long served as a mirror to human feelings, capturing the essence of sorrow, love, anger, and fear through written expression.
For centuries, literature has been used as an avenue to communicate depth of human stories, enabling readers to connect to characters and narratives to a deeply emotional degree [1].
text.formatted: For centuries, literature has been used as an avenue to communicate depth of human stories, enabling readers to connect to characters and narratives to a deeply emotional degree <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Beyond this, literary texts provide insights into the complexities of the human mind by portraying the unconscious motivations, emotional struggles, and interpersonal relationships that shape human behavior.

In line with this, several literary characters have embodied complex psychological experiences allowing readers to examine how unconscious motivations and emotional conflicts have been artistically represented within literary narratives by employing psychoanalytic criticism.

Rooted in the psychoanalytic theories of Sigmund Freud, psychoanalytic criticism posits that human behavior is largely influenced by unresolved conflicts and repressed emotions laid in its unconscious mind [2].
text.formatted: Rooted in the psychoanalytic theories of Sigmund Freud, psychoanalytic criticism posits that human behavior is largely influenced by unresolved conflicts and repressed emotions laid in its unconscious mind <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: Freud argued that when individuals encounter anxiety or emotional distress, the ego unconsciously employs defense mechanisms to protect itself from psychological pain.
These mechanics include denial, displacement, fantasy, and fixation, which allow individuals to cope with excruciating and threatening experiences.

Defense mechanisms, as explained by Freud, were aimed to redirect or disguise these conflicts through symbolic behaviors, recurring patterns, and unconscious expressions rather than eliminating the psychological conflict [3].
text.formatted: Defense mechanisms, as explained by Freud, were aimed to redirect or disguise these conflicts through symbolic behaviors, recurring patterns, and unconscious expressions rather than eliminating the psychological conflict <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, literary texts become valuable sites for examining how characters negotiate emotional trauma through symbolic actions and psychological defenses.

While Freudian defense mechanisms explain how individuals respond to psychological conflict, later psychoanalytic developments provide a deeper understanding of why certain people and objects become emotionally significant.

Object Relations Theory developed by Melani Klein and Donald Winnicott, posits that human beings establish profound emotional attachments to significant others, referred to as objects, and that these internalized relationships continue to influence perception, identity, and behavior throughout life [4].
text.formatted: Object Relations Theory developed by Melani Klein and Donald Winnicott, posits that human beings establish profound emotional attachments to significant others, referred to as objects, and that these internalized relationships continue to influence perception, identity, and behavior throughout life <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Within literary criticism, this theory suggests that physical objects may acquire symbolic psychological value because they become extensions of interpersonal relationships and emotional security.
This perspective complements Freudian psychoanalysis by dissecting how unconscious defenses become attached to symbolic objects that represent love, attachment, and fear of loss.

These psychoanalytic lenses provide a compelling framework for examining Jimmy Alcantar's paired narratives, Red ang Luha ni Michael and Blue ang Kobrekama ni Jake, which portray Ricky and Michael's long-term relationship alongside Ricky's increasingly unstable psychological state.

In the first narrative, Ricky's affectionate act of repainting their refrigerator develops into an obsessive transformation of their home, while the sequel depicts his attempt to construct an ideal family through Jake and the symbolic blue bedspread.

Across both narratives, objects such as the scarlet pain, transformed apartment, imagined family, and blue bedspread become psychological extensions of Ricky's unconscious desire for intimacy, stability, and emotional security.

His responses to rejection, abandonment, and loss likewise reveal unconscious defense mechanisms, suggesting that the narratives extend beyond LGBTQ+ representation toward the psychological processes underlying love and attachment.
Thus, this study investigates how Freudian defense mechanisms and Object Relations Theory are revealed in the characters of Jimmy Alcantara's paired narratives.
Specifically it answers to the following queries: 1.

How are Freudian defense mechanisms, particularly denial, displacement, fantasy, and projection, manifested in Ricky's thoughts, emotions, and behaviors in Jimmy Alcantar's Red ang Luha ni Michael and Blue ang Kobrekama ni Jake?

How do symbolic objects, specifically the scarlet paint, the transformed apartment, the blue bedspread, and Jake, function as psychological extensions of Ricky's emotional attachment to Michael through the perspective of Object Relations Theory?
How do Freudian defense mechanisms and Object Relations Theory collectively explain Ricky's psychological conflicts and emotional attachment as portrayed across the paired narratives?
This study employs qualitative research using literary analysis on the psychoanalytic approach of Jimmy Alcantara's Red ang Luha ni Michael and Blue ang Kobrekama ni Jake.

The analysis primarily uses the four (4) criteria of Freudian defense mechanisms based on psychological responses of Ricky namely: denial, displacement, fantasy, and projection, as avenues in dissecting his emotional conflicts and repressed behaviors.

Further, Object Relations Theory serves as a complementary framework in interpreting Ricky's emotional attachment to Michael and the psychological significance of objects associated with their relationship.
The researchers conducted repeated close readings of the literary texts and identified relevant passages that demonstrate the four selected defense mechanisms.
These textual instances were categorized according to hierarchical defense mechanisms scale of Di Giuseppe and Perry (2021) and interpreted within their narrative contexts.
The analysis focused on characterization, behavior, symbolism, and narrative events without making clinical diagnoses of the literary characters in the paired narratives.

Denial emerges as a significant defense mechanism in the paired narratives of Jimmy Alcantara, particularly in Ricky's persistent refusal to acknowledge aspects of reality that threaten his emotional attachment to Michael.

Di Giuseppe and Perry (2021) describe denial as a defense mechanism that enables the individual to refuse acknowledging an aspect of external reality of personal experiences that would otherwise be apparent to others.
The two narratives reveal Ricky's denial as a progressive event as a way of preserving his preferred version of his relationship and domestic life with Michael.
In the first narrative, Red ang Luha ni Michael, Ricky was already established as a character whose perception does not correspond entirely with the perceptions of those around him.

At the beginning of the narrative, Ricky explains that he and Michael have been together for six years and that their relationship is 'difficult to define' specifically saying, "di kami apektado kung di man namin ma-define ang relasyon namin."
He presents their shared life as natural and harmonious despite acknowledging the fact that their relationship does not conform to a conventional category.
Significantly, Ricky has previously lost his work as a production designer because others consider his ideas and use of colors irrational.
This detail becomes important because it establishes that Ricky's unusual perception of color predates the central incident involving the red paint.
Initially, the response of Ricky to Michael's casual complaint about their aging refrigerator demonstrates an early form of denial.
Michael merely remarks that the refrigerator is becoming rusty and that he feels embarrassed when visitors see it.
This reaction from Michael was taken differently by Ricky, seeing it as an opportunity to surprise Michael by painting the refrigerator with a scarlet red paint.
He convinces himself that Michael will appreciate the change, describing red as dramatic, romantic, and something Michael would "like."
Ricky consequently interprets his own desire as the accurate understanding of Michael's desire.
His interpretation becomes increasingly detached from Michael's actual response.
The denial becomes more evident when the act of painting expands beyond the refrigerator.
Ricky initially intends only to repaint the appliance, but he progressively paints the cupboards, sink, lampshade, furniture, door, ceiling fan, shoes, garden objects, and other parts of the house.

He even recognizes moments when he should stop, telling himself, "Ayoko na, tama na," yet immediately supplies another justification for continuing: the house would look incomplete if only one part were red.
This statement becomes a manifestation of the recognition of excessiveness of Ricky's behavior but suppresses the implication of that recognition by producing another explanation.
The strongest manifestation of denial occurs when Michael finally returns and reflects the transformed environment.
This event prompts Michael to leave and tells Ricky that he is becoming insane, yet Ricky does not respond by reconsidering his behavior.
Instead, he continues to interpret Michael's reaction through the framework of his own reality.
When Michael says that he will leave and return to a friend in Fairview, Ricky remains concerned with the wet paint on Michael's luggage.
More strikingly, when Michael accused him, "Totoo ngang nababaliw ka na," Ricky does not acknowledge the accusation.
He responds by painting Michael's tears read.
This act symbolically converts Michael's emotional rejection into another element of Ricky's red world, thereby allowing Ricky to preserve his preferred interpretation of the relationship.
The same defense becomes more explicit in the second narrative, Blue ang Kobrekama ni Jake.
After Michael confronts Ricky about his behavior and eventually declares, "Hindi na ito anxiety, this is insanity," Ricky responds, "Magaling na ako.
There is nothing wrong with me.
Si Michael ang nababaliw."
Here, denial becomes unmistakably present due to Ricky's rejection of his condition and reverses the accusation onto Michael.
Instead of recognizing the conflict between his perception and Michael's, Ricky maintains his perception of self-stability and that Michael is the one who has become irrational.
Thus, denial functions across the paired narratives as a psychological barrier protecting Ricky from realities that threaten his emotional security.
In Red ang Luha ni Michael, denial allows him to preserve his belief that his transformation of the home they shared is an expression of love that Michael must appreciate.
Consequently, in the second narrative, it enables him to reject the possibility that his perception of Jake and his family life is fundamentally different from Michael's perception.

The progression suggests that denial becomes increasingly consequential: what begins as resistance to Michael's rejection of the red environment eventually becomes resistance to the distinction between internal reality and the external world.

Displacement is evident throughout Jimmy Alcantara's paired narratives as Ricky repeatedly redirects emotional energy arising from his relationship with Michael toward objects, spaces, and activities that he can more easily control.
In psychoanalytic theory, displacement refers to the transfer of an emotion, impulse, or response from its original and potentially threatening target to a less threatening substitute.

Di Giuseppe and Perry (2021) identify displacement as one of the defense mechanisms through which individuals manage psychological conflict by shifting emotional responses away from their original source.

From this perspective, Ricky's fixation on painting may be understood not simply as an artistic preference but as a behavioral outlet through which interpersonal tensions are transformed into controllable material actions.
The process initially emerges from Michael's complaint about their rusty refrigerator.
Although Michael's concern is relatively ordinary and practical, Ricky interprets it as an opportunity to demonstrate his affection, thinking, "Ito na ang pagkakataon para sorpresahin si Mike."
Instead of addressing the concern through direct communication or simply replacing the damaged appliance, Ricky invests himself in repainting it.
His choice of scarlet red gives the action an emotional dimension because the refrigerator becomes associated with his desire to please Michael.
The appliance consequently shifts from being an ordinary household object to becoming a target for Ricky's emotional investment.
The displacement becomes more apparent when Ricky's activity extends beyond the refrigerator.
After experiencing satisfaction from painting it, he begins repainting other parts of the household, including cupboards, the sink, lampshades, picture frames, flower pots, plants, and other objects.
His admission, "Naa-addict na ako sa ginagawa ko," signals an important change in behavior.
What began as a response to Michael's dissatisfaction develops into a self-sustaining activity.
The original interpersonal concern becomes increasingly distant as Ricky transfers his emotional energy toward transforming the physical environment.
This expansion is particularly significant because many of the objects Ricky paints are connected to Michael.
His decision to paint Michael's slippers, bags, belts, and other belongings demonstrates that the objects have acquired emotional significance through their association with his partner.

This interpretation may be strengthened through Object Relations Theory, which emphasizes the psychological importance of internalized relationships and the ways individuals invest in people and associated objects with emotional meaning.
Thomas et al. (2023) explain that object relations perspectives examine how relationships with significant others become internalized and subsequently influence emotional experiences and behavior.
Thus, Ricky's manipulation of objects associated with Michael can be interpreted as an attempt to preserve an external representation of the relationship.
The scarlet paint consequently functions as more than a decorative medium.
It becomes a vehicle through which Ricky externalizes and manages feelings that are difficult to negotiate directly within the relationship.
By repeatedly applying the same color to objects connected to Michael and their shared domestic life, he creates a physical environment that reflects his preferred emotional reality.
The act of painting therefore provides Ricky with a sense of agency: unlike interpersonal relationships, objects can be altered according to his wishes.
The physical environment becomes controllable in a way that Michael's feelings and decisions are not.
The displacement becomes increasingly pronounced as Ricky begins painting objects that have little or no connection to the original problem.
His activity expands to the garden, plants, telephone, and eventually even the postman.
At this point, the behavior has moved substantially away from Michael's initial complaint about the refrigerator.
Ricky's explanation that he paints the postman's face so that he will not appear anemic further illustrates how his preferred aesthetic reality begins to govern his perception of the world.
The narrative thus presents a progressive movement from a specific interpersonal stimulus toward increasingly unrelated targets.

Psychoanalytically, this progression suggests that the painting activity has become a means through which Ricky manages an emotional tension that can no longer be contained within the original situation.
The most significant manifestation occurs when Michael himself becomes incorporated into Ricky's symbolic world.
After returning to the transformed apartment, Michael reacts with shock and distress and attempts to leave.
Rather than responding to Michael's emotional reaction through direct communication, Ricky paints Michael's tears red.
This moment marks a significant transformation in the pattern of displacement.
The emotional response that should become the subject of interpersonal communication is instead absorbed into Ricky's established symbolic system.
Michael's sadness is no longer treated as an independent emotional reality; it becomes another element that Ricky can transform through the color red.
The action consequently demonstrates how Ricky's psychological strategy has shifted from modifying objects to modifying the visible expression of another person's emotions.
The second narrative reinforces this pattern by showing Ricky repeatedly altering Michael's domestic environment.

Changes involving the living room, component system, bedsheets, and pillowcases suggest that the manipulation of physical surroundings has become an established means through which Ricky negotiates emotional tension.

The refrigerator is particularly significant because it becomes a contested object: what initially served as an expression of Ricky's affection eventually becomes a source of conflict when Michael attempts to remove the paint.
The object therefore embodies the changing nature of their relationship.
Its transformation reflects Ricky's attachment, while Michael's attempt to restore it reflects his resistance to the reality that Ricky has constructed.
From an Object Relations perspective, this conflict illustrates the psychological significance that ordinary objects may acquire when they become associated with emotionally important relationships.

The refrigerator, household belongings, beddings, and other domestic objects are not significant merely because of their material functions; within Ricky's psychological world, they become connected to his relationship with Michael.
His repeated attempts to transform them can therefore be understood as attempts to maintain an external representation of attachment.
By controlling the objects surrounding the relationship, Ricky symbolically attempts to preserve a sense of relational stability that he cannot guarantee through Michael himself.
Across the paired narratives, displacement therefore operates as both a psychological defense and a narrative device.
Ricky's emotional conflicts are seldom confronted directly.
Instead, they are transferred into colors, household objects, domestic spaces, personal belongings, and eventually representations of Michael's own emotional experience.
The red paint becomes an external manifestation of an internal struggle: Ricky attempts to make the external world correspond to the emotional reality he desires.
However, this strategy produces a paradox.

The very mechanism that initially allows Ricky to express affection and manage emotional tension gradually distances him from Michael because the symbolic world he creates increasingly takes precedence over Michael's actual feelings and perceptions.
Thus, displacement in the paired narratives does not simply demonstrate Ricky's tendency to redirect emotion toward objects.
It reveals a deeper psychological struggle between the desire to preserve attachment and the inability to control another person's emotional reality.
Ricky can repaint a refrigerator, transform an apartment, and alter objects associated with Michael, but he cannot determine whether Michael will accept the world he has created.
His increasing investment in controllable objects consequently reflects an attempt to compensate for the uncontrollable nature of human attachment.

Through the combined perspectives of Freudian psychoanalysis and Object Relations Theory, the red-painted environment can therefore be interpreted as an externalized psychological space in which Ricky attempts to preserve, control, and materialize a relationship that is increasingly unstable in reality.

Fantasy becomes the most prominent defense mechanism in Blue ang Kobrekama ni Jake, where Ricky constructs and sustains an imagined family life that compensates for emotional needs that cannot be adequately satisfied in his actual relationship with Michael.
Di Giuseppe and Perry (2021) describe autistic or schizoid fantasy as the use of excessive fantasy as a substitute for human relationships, direct action, or problem solving.
Fantasy may provide temporary gratification by allowing an individual to imagine a solution to an interpersonal conflict without confronting the actual difficulty.
This concept is particularly applicable to Ricky's treatment of Jake, whose presence allows him to construct an idealized family that increasingly diverges from Michael's perception of reality.
The foundation for this fantasy is established before Jake's arrival.
Ricky explains that he and Michael cannot have children and describes their inability to have a child as a consequence of their circumstances.
After nearly six years of living together, however, Michael proposes adoption: "Ampon tayo, gusto mo?"
Ricky immediately agrees.
The adoption therefore becomes a concrete possibility for fulfilling a previously unfulfilled aspect of their relationship.
Yet Ricky's subsequent behavior demonstrates that he invests the child with meanings that extend beyond the actual act of adoption.
When Ricky brings the child home, the baby is immediately incorporated into his imagined family structure.
The child is placed in a prepared bed with a blue bedspread, and Ricky describes the baby as resembling Michael.
He anticipates that Michael will be happy because the child is a boy, which is what he believes Michael wants.
Ricky then addresses the baby directly and assigns him the name Jake.
More significantly, he tells the baby, "Kami na ang mga magulang mo" and insists that the child is no longer an adopted child but belongs to them.
These declarations demonstrate how quickly Ricky transforms the child from an adopted infant into the embodiment of an ideal family.
Ricky's fantasy becomes especially evident in his insistence that Jake's identity should conform to the family he imagines.
He tells the baby to think of himself as having come from them and explains that they are his parents.
The statement "Hindi ka ampon" is particularly significant because the reality of adoption is replaced with a more emotionally satisfying narrative of biological and familial belonging.
The fantasy therefore does not simply invent a child; it reconstructs the meaning of the child's existence so that the child can occupy the precise emotional role Ricky needs.

Although Ricky interprets Michael's emotional response to the child as evidence of happiness, Michael eventually rejects the arrangement and tells Ricky, "isoli mo siya, hindi natin kailangan ng kasama."
Ricky does not accept this statement.
Instead, he dismisses Michael's reaction as another instance of "drama" and continues caring for the baby as though the family he imagines remains intact.
This is important because fantasy becomes a substitute for direct engagement with the actual conflict.
Ricky does not negotiate the disagreement with Michael; he retreats further into the imagined family.
The narrative's final revelation makes this defense particularly powerful.
During the confrontation, Michael takes the baby from Ricky and throws it to the floor.
Ricky experiences the event as the destruction of his child and responds emotionally to the injured body.
He speaks to the baby, asking it to open its eyes and tell him that it loves its daddy.
Only after this emotional scene does the narrator reveal, "Nangiti ako.
Ibinalik ko ang mga baterya sa dating ayos."
The batteries retroactively establish that Jake is not the living child Ricky believes him to be but an object that Ricky has incorporated into his psychological reality.
The revelation transforms Jake into the clearest representation of fantasy in the paired narratives.
The object becomes a substitute for the interpersonal relationship Ricky desires but cannot secure.

Through Object Relations Theory, Jake may therefore be interpreted as more than an imaginary child: he becomes a symbolic object through which Ricky attempts to preserve an idealized relationship with Michael.
The blue bedspread reinforces this interpretation because the color and domestic setting establish an environment associated with the peaceful family life Ricky wishes to construct.
Consequently, fantasy in the narrative functions not simply as escapism but as a psychological substitute for an unattainable interpersonal reality.
Ricky's imagined family temporarily provides the intimacy, belonging, and companionship he fears losing.
However, because the fantasy increasingly replaces rather than negotiates external reality, it ultimately deepens his isolation.
Alcantara thus uses Jake to demonstrate how an internally constructed emotional world can become more compelling to Ricky than the reality recognized by everyone around him.
Projection is manifested most clearly in Ricky's attribution of his own psychological disturbance to Michael, particularly in the latter part of Blue ang Kobrekama ni Jake.
According to Di Giuseppe and Perry (2021), projection occurs when an individual attributes one's own unacknowledged feelings, impulses, or thoughts to another person.
In Ricky's case, projection becomes evident when his perception of Michael increasingly incorporates the very psychological instability that the narrative has been establishing in Ricky himself.
A significant basis for this interpretation appears in the first story.
Ricky has already been described as someone whose artistic ideas and use of color have been regarded by others as irrational.
He reports losing his work as a production designer because his employers considered his colors and concepts unacceptable and referred to him as "nahihibang."
Yet Ricky narrates these events without critically examining the possibility that others' perceptions might contain some truth.
Instead, he maintains his own interpretation of his behavior.
This pattern intensifies when Michael confronts him in Red ang Luha ni Michael.
After seeing the completely transformed apartment, Michael tells Ricky that he is becoming insane and says that he will return him to the basement.
Ricky does not explicitly acknowledge Michael's assessment.
Instead, he responds by painting Michael's tears red.

The act itself may be read primarily as displacement, but it also establishes the narrative condition necessary for projection: Ricky consistently treats Michael's responses as the problem while preserving his own perception as reasonable.
The clearest evidence emerges in Blue ang Kobrekama ni Jake.

As Michael becomes increasingly distressed by Ricky's behavior and eventually attempts to remove the baby from the house, Ricky interprets Michael's actions as evidence that Michael himself has become irrational.
When Michael declares, "Hindi na ito anxiety, this is insanity," Ricky immediately responds: "Magaling na ako.
There is nothing wrong with me.
Si Mike ang nababaliw."
The structure of this response is significant.
Ricky first denies the possibility that anything is wrong with him and then attributes the psychological problem to Michael.

This moment corresponds closely to the function of projection described by Di Giuseppe and Perry (2021), in which the individual externalizes psychological material that is difficult to acknowledge internally.

Ricky's accusation that Michael is "the one going crazy" is especially revealing because the narrative has provided substantial evidence of Ricky's increasingly distorted perception: he interprets an object as his child, treats it as a living infant, and maintains that it belongs within his family even when Michael rejects the interpretation.
Ricky's projection also appears in his interpretation of Michael's motives.
After Michael rejects Jake, Ricky interprets his partner's response as unreasonable hostility toward the child.
He asks, "Di ba sabi mo'y okay ang bata sa bahay?
Ngayon, bakit ka nag-iingay?"
Rather than interpreting Michael's distress as a reaction to Ricky's behavior, Ricky frames Michael as the source of the conflict.

Later, when Michael becomes aggressive and attempts to remove Jake, Ricky fears that Michael has also become mentally unstable: "huwag mong sabihing nababaliw na rin si Mike, huwag mong sabihing nahawaan ko siya."

The latter statement is particularly interesting because it briefly introduces self-awareness-Ricky recognizes the possibility that his own instability has influenced the situation-but he quickly returns to viewing Michael as the one who is "crazy."
Projection therefore works together with denial.
Denial prevents Ricky from acknowledging his own psychological disturbance, while projection allows him to relocate that disturbance onto Michael.
The two defenses consequently reinforce one another.
Ricky can maintain the belief that he is "well" precisely because the perceived problem has been transferred to someone else.
However, the textual evidence for projection should be treated more cautiously than that for denial, displacement, and fantasy.
Ricky's statement that Michael is "crazy" can also be read as an extension of denial rather than pure projection.
The distinction rests on whether the accusation is interpreted as Ricky attributing his own unacknowledged psychological state to Michael.
For this reason, projection should be presented as a secondary but significant manifestation, rather than claiming that every instance of Ricky's disagreement with Michael constitutes projection.
Taken together, the evidence demonstrates that projection contributes to the progressive collapse of Ricky's relationship with external reality.
By attributing his own disturbance to Michael, Ricky preserves the internal world he has constructed around their relationship.
Michael consequently becomes not only the person Ricky fears losing but also the person onto whom Ricky transfers the psychological conflict he cannot acknowledge within himself.

In conclusion, the analysis demonstrates that Jimmy Alcantara's Red ang Luha ni Michael and Blue ang Kobrekama ni Jake portray Ricky's psychological conflict through the defense mechanisms of denial, displacement, fantasy, and projection, which shape his responses to rejection, emotional insecurity, and the fear of losing Michael.

His denial allows him to resist threatening realities, while displacement redirects his emotional conflict toward the objects and spaces associated with his relationship; fantasy enables him to construct an idealized family through Jake, and projection allows him to externalize his own psychological conflict onto Michael.

Complementing these mechanisms, Object Relations Theory reveals how the red paint, domestic space, blue bedspread, and Jake acquire psychological significance as extensions or representations of Ricky's attachment to Michael.

Taken together, the findings suggest that Alcantara uses these symbolic objects and defensive responses to portray the gradual entanglement of Ricky's internal desires with external reality, illustrating how an intense need for attachment and emotional security can transform ordinary objects into substitutes for human relationships and ultimately contribute to psychological fragmentation.
